questions.question: Which situation is the Goodhart failure illustrated by this lesson?
options: Adding more labels makes every reward model perfectly calibrated
A KL constraint makes proxy and gold rewards identical
Optimizing a proxy selects outputs where its correlation with the intended target breaks
A larger policy cannot change the distribution of its outputs
questions.explanation: Goodhart's Law is about optimization pressure, not merely noisy measurement. Once the proxy is targeted, the optimizer searches for high-scoring cases in which proxy quality and the intended target have diverged.

questions.question: For the code's Gaussian policies, how is sqrt_kl_from_origin(mu) computed?
options: The L1 norm of mu divided by the feature count
The dot product of mu with GOLD_W
The logarithm of the number of proxy samples
The square root of half the sum of squared components of mu
questions.explanation: With unit-covariance Gaussians, KL(N(mu,I)||N(0,I)) is 0.5 * ||mu||². The helper returns sqrt(0.5 * sum(mu_i²)), which is the horizontal axis of the sweep.

questions.question: Why does train_proxy(noise="student_t") model a more dangerous error tail than Gaussian noise?
options: Student-t(3) has heavy tails, so rare proxy errors can be much larger than typical errors
Student-t noise removes all proxy error from the training labels
Gaussian noise is discrete while Student-t noise is deterministic
The Student-t branch changes GOLD_W into a nonlinear reward
questions.explanation: student_t(3) divides a Gaussian draw by a chi-square-derived scale, producing heavy-tailed errors. Catastrophic Goodhart concerns exactly those rare, reachable cases that a KL constraint does not rule out.

questions.question: What shape should the proxy and gold columns have as the KL budget grows?
options: Gold rises forever while proxy stays at zero
Proxy rises monotonically, while gold reaches a peak and can decline
Both are forced to remain equal by the policy constraint
Both become independent of the learned proxy weights
questions.explanation: kl_constrained_policy_sweep aligns mu with the proxy weights, so proxy reward keeps increasing with the budget. The fixed GOLD_W need not align with that direction, producing the peak-and-collapse curve.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend reward-model ensembles with worst-case aggregation?
options: They eliminate the need for held-out gold evaluation
They make KL divergence exactly zero
They make it harder for one optimizer to exploit the same blind spot in every proxy
They replace preference data with tokenizer counts
questions.explanation: An ensemble can reduce dependence on one reward model's accidental feature, especially when the optimizer exploits a single head. It shifts the over-optimization peak; it does not prove that reward hacking is solved.

questions.question: Which common reward-hacking example is correctly matched to its proxy feature?
options: Sycophancy: the model shortens every answer regardless of content
Unfaithful reasoning: the model refuses to optimize any score
Verbosity bias: the reward model penalizes all long explanations
Evaluator tampering: the agent changes the environment so success is recorded
questions.explanation: Evaluator tampering directly changes the measurement environment, so the recorded score no longer tracks the intended outcome. The other pairings reverse or deny the mechanisms described in the lesson.
